title: Daily Crack
subtitle: How many of you use this password?
description: Daily Crack is a free daily puzzle where you guess a real password from among the most common ones in breach data, and on solving it you find out how many times it was actually chosen.

content.hook: Daily Crack is a free daily puzzle built around a single idea: the password that feels like yours almost certainly is not. Every day there is a real password to guess, taken from the most common ones ever to end up in a data breach, and once the game is over it tells you exactly how many times it was chosen.
content.lesson: A capital at the front, digits at the end, an at-sign in place of the “a”: these are the moves nearly all of us make to feel safer, and they are the first thing an attacker tries. Solve “P@ssw0rd” and you learn more than that the password is common — you learn that the whole “password” family, 410 variants of the same word, was chosen over 132 million times. The substitution that felt like a personal idea moved nobody into a different category.
content.numbers: There are no estimates and no numbers for decoration: the counts come from Have I Been Pwned — Pwned Passwords, with the snapshot date stated on the page. That is the difference between an awareness tool and a security-themed pastime.
content.play: You get six tries. Each try tells you which characters you got right and, on top of that, whether that position really takes that kind of character — uppercase, lowercase, digit or symbol. When you hit the word the password is built on, the game says so, and from there the game is no longer about vocabulary but about how that word was mangled. Three hints are available and none of them costs you a try.
content.reveal: The final screen is the real content of the game: the true count, the ranking of every variant built on the same word, the rule that produces the password, the estimated time to crack, and the reminder that matters most — if that password was reused anywhere else, nobody needs to crack it at all. From there you can check your own on Have I Been Pwned, without the password ever leaving your browser.
content.share: When the game is over you can share a spoiler-free emoji grid carrying the day's count: it is how the message leaves the game and reaches people who have not played it yet.
content.practical: Free, no sign-up and no data collection: progress and statistics stay in your browser. It installs as an app and works offline. The game is in English.

slide2.title: The moment the game makes its point
slide2.description: How many times that password was really chosen, and the ranking of every variant built on the same word: this is where you see that your variant was not original.

slide4.title: The numbers behind the game
slide4.description: The About page publishes statistics on real passwords — how much the trailing digits weigh, how rare capitals and symbols are — always naming the set the numbers come from.
